extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, comparative government, and civic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-length analysis of the political advantages and defects of democratic government (with sustained comparison to aristocracy), covering foreign policy, legislation, public officers, patriotism, rights, and respect for law, with examples drawn from the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent alliances; prefer temporary alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: The nation should avoid permanent entangling alliances and observe existing engagements in their genuine sense; it is unnecessary and unwise to extend them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the country in a respectable defensive posture and trust temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies. Washington's maxim: habitual hatred or fondness enslaves a nation to passion and leads it astray from duty and interest. Practical example: maintain neutrality in European internal dissensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not solicit foreign privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans ought never to solicit any privileges from foreign nations, so as not to be obliged to grant similar privileges themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim (attributed to Jefferson) is offered as a foreign-policy rule to avoid reciprocal obligations or compromises of independence; it reduces causes for diplomatic entanglement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect neutrality regarding other powers' internal dissensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The true interest of the Americans consists in a perfect neutrality with regard to the internal dissensions of the European Powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Union has no powerful continental neighbors and is geographically removed from Old World passions, abstaining from interference is the prudent foreign policy; the country's role is more to avoid meddling than to exert activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish a law's ends from its means when evaluating legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering laws one must distinguish between the end at which they aim and the means by which they are directed to that end, between their absolute and their relative excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law may be well drawn (effective) yet have a bad purpose; the more efficacious such a law, the greater the mischief. Evaluation must therefore weigh both purpose and efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic legislation should favor the greatest number
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic laws generally tend to promote the welfare of the greatest possible number because they emanate from the majority of citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as the central advantage of democracy: even if laws are imperfect or changeable, their purpose aligns with the majority's interest rather than a minority's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic legislation tends to concentrate wealth and power
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws under aristocracy tend to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of the minority, because an aristocracy is by nature a minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While aristocracies may be more skillful lawmakers, their ends often favor their own order; thus legislative expertise can produce outcomes harmful to the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of democratic flexibility: ability to commit and repair faults
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic government can commit faults by passing bad or imperfect laws but has the capacity to repair them later; this flexibility is a key advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a polity can survive the transitory action of bad laws, the general tendency of democratic legislation to favor the majority will conduce to prosperity over time; the capacity to change laws is a safety valve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic public officers' interests align with majority
rubrics_metrics.description: In a democratic state public officers have no permanent interests distinct from those of the majority; their interests are identified with those of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individuals are less talented or moral than aristocratic counterparts, because their tenure is shorter and their interests conflate with the majority, they are less likely to concert permanent measures harmful to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short tenure limits the harm of bad magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Maladministration by a democratic magistrate is an isolated fact that only occurs during the short period for which he is elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because corruption and incapacity do not act as enduring common interests in democracies, individual vices rarely become systemic; rivals within the system tend to unmask and check one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic officeholders may form long-lasting, harmful coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies public men are swayed by the interest of their order, which serves as a common and lasting bond that unites them and may not coincide with the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shared interest connects them to a portion of the community and to future generations, producing enduring policies that can sacrifice the majority's welfare; even talented or virtuous aristocrats can unconsciously fashion society to their order's ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign politics require discretion, perseverance, secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign politics demand qualities (regulating details, perseverance in a design, secrecy, patience) in which democracies are deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracies are prone to passion and caprice, cannot combine measures with secrecy, and will not await consequences patiently; such defects make democratic governments often inferior at foreign policy compared to aristocracies or strong individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity of purpose is an aristocratic advantage for great designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocratic institutions afford an absolute fixity of purpose—numerous enough to resist fleeting passions but small enough not to yield to them—which enables conceiving and executing vast designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This collective permanence yields energy and continuity across generations, helping states achieve long-range projects and predominant positions; contrasted with the volatility of popular majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate reflective (rational) patriotism over instinctive patriotism
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two species of patriotism: instinctive (faith-like, sentimental) and reflective (rational, tied to laws and rights); nations ought to strive to acquire the second when the first has disappeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflective patriotism is less ardent but more lasting and productive—it is nurtured by laws and civil rights and links personal interest to the country's welfare; instinctive patriotism may save a state in emergencies but will not sustain prosperity in peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach notion of rights by granting practical exercise of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The best means to inculcate the notion of rights is to invest members of the community with the peaceful exercise of certain rights (political and property rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like a child learning to respect others' possessions by having toys, citizens learn to respect political and property rights when they themselves hold and exercise them. Extension of rights thus fosters mutual respect and civic restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend political rights to foster civic zeal and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Making citizens partakers in government increases civic zeal; the number of citizens who engage will rise as political rights are extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic zeal (the union of private with public interests) is often inseparable from the exercise of political rights; extending rights is recommended to bind personal interest to public welfare, though timing and readiness matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious: granting rights too early risks abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: When political rights are first granted to previously unentitled people, they may be abused—the newly enfranchised are like children learning their place in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'apprenticeship of liberty' is arduous; the states where citizens have enjoyed rights longest make the best use of them. Expansion of rights is beneficial but must consider citizens' maturity and social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for law strengthened by popular origin and personal stake
rubrics_metrics.description: Law gains authority when it expresses the determination of the whole people and when each person is personally interested in enforcing obedience, because laws originate in his own authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular origin overawes contesting imagination; citizens comply not only because a law is majority-made but because they see it as a contract to which they are a party. This explains the strong respect for law in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property ownership fosters respect for others' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When individuals possess property, they learn the value of rights and therefore are less inclined to attack property or rights in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical claim: absence of widespread pauperism (as in the U.S. at the time) reduces complaints against property; those with something to lose are more likely to respect legal and property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's advantage: benefits the greatest number, not all classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantage of democracy is its contribution to the well-being of the greatest possible number, not the prosperity of every social class equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No political form equally favors all classes; democracies protect the majority's interests, whereas aristocracies may systematically favor a minority even when laws are expert and stable.

rubrics_metrics.name: National attachment often mixed with self-interest (cupidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States patriotic attachment often combines with personal interest: citizens equate national prosperity with their private advantage and act accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This self-interested patriotism creates strong civic participation but also an irritable national pride that resists criticism; Americans may defend their country reflexively because its fortunes are felt as personal.
